case.title: Disputed recording 2
case.brief: A 8-minute indoor phone video is offered as evidence. It is said to start at 11:07:07 UTC on Sunday 08 November 2026. Establish independently when it was recorded and whether the stated time holds.

evidence.label: Indoor video, 8 min (ceiling strip lights)
evidence.source: supplied by a party to the dispute

text: Starting by looking at the scene and probing signals.

input.reason: Need to see light sources and any on-screen clock before choosing a channel.
Determine which channel (flicker vs hum) carries usable grid signal.

text: Dark room lit only by ceiling strip lights, no windows or on-screen clock. Light flicker is strong (72% usable, 19 dB) vs weak audio hum (20%), so video is the channel.

input.reason: Flicker is strong and grid-like while audio hum is only 20% usable.

result.ELEXON_15s_remote: any date via the Elexon API (fetched on demand, ~15 s cadence, noisier)

input.reason: Only Elexon 15 s covers Nov 2026; start with a window around the stated 11:07:07.

text: The timestamp I was given, 11:47:08, is 40 minutes and 1 second later than the figure stated, so I'll challenge that claim.
Strong lock at 11:47:08, about 40 minutes after the stated start. Challenging it.

input.reason: Top candidate 0.969 with 0.146 margin is 40 min off the claim; must test before relying on it.

input.headline: The flicker of the room's lights matches the national grid record at 11:47:08 UTC on 8 Nov 2026. That is about 40 minutes after the stated 11:07:07 start, and the stated time does not match.
input.difference: The recording started about 40 minutes (40 min 1 s) later than stated, on the same day.
input.what_it_means: The video was very likely made on the stated day, Sunday 8 November, but around 11:47 rather than 11:07. Anything that depends on the video showing the scene at 11:07–11:15 is not supported by this timing evidence. This does not explain why the times differ. It could be a wrong phone clock, a mistake in how the time was stated, or something else. The person who supplied the video should be asked to explain it.
findings: Scene: a dark indoor room lit only by ceiling strip lights. There are no windows and no clock on screen, so the electrical flicker of the lights is the only independent timing source.
The light flicker gave a strong grid signal: 72% of the clip was usable. The audio hum was weak, with only 20% usable, so the video channel was used.
Searching the national grid record for 08:00–14:00 on 8 Nov found one clear best match at 11:47:08 UTC (score 0.969 out of 1). The next-best time scored only 0.82.
Splitting the clip in two, each half points to the same start time within 1 second. This argues against editing or splicing.
The match falls away sharply just seconds from 11:47:08, and scores only 0.39 at one minute off. The stated 11:07 is nowhere near any good match.
The best matches on the three days either side (5–11 Nov) all score lower (best 0.886), so the recording fits 8 Nov best.
Caveat: the only grid record available for November 2026 is the 15-second Elexon series, which is coarser than the 1-second archive. Because of the clear margins, this does not change the conclusion.

Caveat: the evidence is marked as an excerpt covering seconds 270–750. If the stated time was meant to be the start of a longer original file, the gap is about 35½ minutes rather than 40. The video still does not match the stated time either way.
next_steps: Ask the person who supplied the video to explain the roughly 40-minute gap, and to confirm whether 11:07:07 was the start of this clip or of a longer original file.
Get the original, unedited file from the phone with its metadata, and check the phone's clock setting against network time.
If other footage or records place events at 11:07 or 11:47, compare them with this result.
Treat this as one strand of evidence that informs the decision. It is not, on its own, a finding of wrongdoing.
